newsitem.title: BELGIUM: British beef ban off EU farm agenda on Monday.
newsitem.headline: British beef ban off EU farm agenda on Monday.

text.p: The worldwide ban on British beef exports will for the first time in many months not be up for discusssion at a low-key meeting on Monday of European Union farm ministers, EU diplomats said.
But they added that ministers will receive at the half-day meeting, their first in 1997, a progress report on proposals to introduce cattle passports and beef labels.

"There is nothing sufficiently important now to justify raising it (the ban) at (EU Farm) Council level," said a diplomat, noting that Britain submits fortnightly progress reports to the EU's executive European Commission.

The next step in Britain's campaign to lift the worldwide beef export ban will be British farm minister Douglas Hogg's presentation, possibly at the end of January, to exempt certified herds from the embargo.

The EU imposed the ban in March 1996 after the British government caused consumer panic by disclosing that the disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE), could be transmitted to humans as Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease CJD).
Most BSE cases, some 165,000, have been reported in Britain.
Northern Irish grass-fed herds, which are tracked from birth by a computerised system, are likely to be the first to be exempted from the ban, officials said.

But they added that the British proposals would first have to be examined by various EU scientific and other committees before being sent to the European Commission for approval, which could take several months.

Diplomats said Dutch Farm Minister Jozias Van Aartsen, whose country took over the rotating EU presidency on January 1, is expected to tell ministers on Monday that the cattle passport and beef label proposals, aimed at restoring consumer confidence, require more work.
"Progress has been made but details, such as whether cattle passports and a computer data base are both needed, still have to be settled," said a Dutch official.

Several member states are pressing for EU financial aid in setting up computerised systems to identify cattle and track their movements and have complained that the January 1998 deadline was too early.
It would be compulsory for all cattle to have ear tags and have passports and for farmers to keep up to date registers.
On beef labelling, countries are split over whether this should be voluntary or compulsory and what details -- such as birthplace, feeding and slaughtering -- should be included.
Various countries, including Germany, France and Britain, are pressing for an early agreement, possibly in February, so as to reassure consumers.
